name: Adam Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Adam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI firms, employers or government, and this conversation is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Coombe & Hale, an agency in a small coastal town that covers about twenty villages. I sell cottages, farmhouses and the odd barn conversion, and I look after some holiday lets too. A day can be forty miles of driving, two viewings, a valuation with a farmer's widow over tea, and an evening of paperwork.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the area, which lanes flood and which wells run dry in August, because buyers from the city never think to ask. What wears me out is the paperwork at the end of the day, the forms and the chasing. I live with my partner Grace, who's a teaching assistant, and we've got about five months saved, which feels okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought: useful for a few chores, nothing more. I use the AI writer now and then for property descriptions, and it's handy but you have to fix it. I'd say that to the lads at the cricket club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job's safe in this world. Country houses need someone who knows the land, and the clients are mostly older people who want a face. My money's fine, Grace's job is steady, and the rent's not crazy here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and maybe use the AI tools a bit more for the end-of-day paperwork to get home earlier. I'd keep saving towards a deposit, two hundred and fifty a month. I'd put my name forward for the branch's senior role in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Life ticks along, and that's what I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything weighing on you, even if AI changes little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The housing market in the villages is slow, because so many places are holiday homes now. But the holiday lets give us steady fees, so the branch is alright. I wouldn't call it a worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the hour you saved on paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get home in time for cricket nets on Thursdays. Honestly, that'd be the biggest change. Grace would like me home earlier too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good agents will adapt like they always have. I'd say it at the office and to my dad, who still thinks computers are a fad. I'd keep it upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the town agencies merge and the office work gets done by software. Bookings, enquiries, holiday-let bookings, those are exactly the tasks on your card. I'd keep my job because of the area knowledge, but the junior staff and the girl on reception might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training when the firm brings the tools in and use them properly once I've seen they work. I'd ask Coombe & Hale to let me take over more holiday-let management, the hands-on side, checking properties and dealing with cleaners. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's business, firms will always use what's cheaper. I'd rather the government stayed out and people were helped to train on the job, like apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the receptionist might go. Would you say anything to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Megan on reception to learn the holiday-let side with me. It's hands-on and the robots aren't there yet. I'd want to help, not just watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast and nobody's ready, which would be true. I'd say it at the cricket club bar. I'd also say the countryside will last longer than the cities, though I'm not sure of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, by 2028 the valuations, the adverts, the haggling over price would all be AI. What's left is the driving and the walking round barns, and that lasts till about 2031. After that I'd have nothing to sell that a machine can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my dad within the month about joining Young & Son, his building firm. Building is hands-on, so it buys me a few more years. I'd keep working at Coombe & Hale part-time while I learned, and we'd keep the savings for the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. But having my dad's building firm there is like a rope to hold onto.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Grace say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say do it, she's always said I'd be good with my hands. Her job in the school is people-facing, so it should last a while. She'd keep us afloat during the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Building gets robots in 2031 on this card. Doesn't that just push the problem back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, three years. But in three years I'd have a trade, and someone has to run the robots on site, at least at first. I'd take three years over nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if you start now. I'd tell younger agents to get a practical skill. I'd also say it at the cricket club, because half the lads are in office jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is enough to learn building properly with my dad before 2031, and then I'd have the trade until robots arrive around 2034. It's a narrow window, but it's a real one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Coombe & Hale for a year or two and save, then start a part-time building course in 2028. I'd work Saturdays with Dad from next spring to learn on the job. Grace and I would hold off buying a house until I'd made the switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I know what I'd be doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not switch straight away, if you know it's coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like to see it happen first. If AGI looks real by 2028, I'd go. If it's still hype, I'd stay in agency work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farmhouses, the people. Sitting in a kitchen hearing about three generations on the farm. Building's good work, but you don't get stories like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, so make sensible plans. I'd tell Megan and the juniors the same. I'd try not to scare anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay an agent for most of the decade and maybe buy a house with Grace. Then I'd move into building or property maintenance around 2033. A decade is time to have a good run at both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Coombe & Hale and go for the senior job. We'd buy a cottage in the next few years while I've got steady pay. I'd do a weekend building course with Dad's help around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than anything. It's far off, but I'd keep thinking about it on the long drives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the ten years change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably get married and buy the house first. Grace wants a garden, and the cottages up by the church come up now and then. Then children, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep saving, but maybe put a bit into a pension now, since I'm switching later. My dad never had a pension, and I don't want to end up like that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to change everything in a year. What would help is support for small family firms like Dad's to take on adult apprentices, so people like me can learn a trade on a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What happens to the villages. If everyone's out of work, nobody's buying cottages, and the holiday-let owners sell up. My job depends on the whole place doing alright.
